l: woman (with ten drachma coins), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The woman who loses one of her ten drachma coins lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and seeks diligently until she finds it. She then calls her friends and neighbors to rejoice with her.

l: lost drachma coin (woman's coin), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: One of the woman's ten drachma coins is lost and is found after she lights a lamp, sweeps, and searches. Its finding prompts her to call others to rejoice, and Jesus compares this to the joy of the angels of God over one repenting sinner.

l: father (of the two sons), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The father divides his livelihood between his two sons when the younger asks for his share. When the younger son returns, the father sees him far off, is moved with compassion, runs, embraces and kisses him, has him clothed with the best robe, a ring and sandals, and orders the fattened calf killed. He then goes out and begs the angry elder son to come in, telling him that all that is his is the elder son's and that celebrating was appropriate because his brother was dead and is alive, lost and found.

l: younger son (prodigal), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The younger son asks for his share of the property, travels to a far country, and wastes it with riotous living. After a famine leaves him feeding pigs and hungry, he comes to himself, resolves to return and ask to be made a hired servant, and confesses his sin to his father. His father receives him and restores him, calling him dead and alive again, lost and found.

l: elder son, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The elder son, in the field, hears music and dancing and learns from a servant that his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed. He becomes angry, refuses to go in, and complains to his father that he has served for years and never disobeyed yet never received even a goat, while his brother who devoured the property with prostitutes got the calf. The father answers that he is always with him and that all that is his is the son's.

l: celebration (feast for the returned son), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: The father orders a celebration with the fattened calf, best robe, ring and sandals for the returned younger son, and they begin to celebrate with music and dancing. The elder son's anger at it prompts the father to explain that it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad because the brother was dead and is alive, lost and found.

l: repentance, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 15
s: Jesus says there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance, and joy in the presence of God's angels over one sinner repenting. In the third parable the younger son's decision to return and confess his sin against heaven and his father shows it, and it is met with welcome and celebration.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: Jesus tells his disciples a parable of a rich man's manager who, accused of wasting possessions and facing dismissal, reduces the debts owed to his lord so that debtors will receive him later; the lord commends his shrewdness. Jesus then teaches about faithfulness in little and much, and says no one can serve both God and Mammon. The money-loving Pharisees scoff, and Jesus says God knows their hearts, that the law and prophets lasted until John, that the law will not fail, and that divorcing and remarrying is adultery. He then tells of a rich man who lived in luxury and the beggar Lazarus; after death Lazarus is comforted at Abraham's bosom while the rich man suffers in Hades, and Abraham refuses his pleas, saying his five brothers have Moses and the prophets.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: Jesus tells his disciples the parable of the dishonest manager and teaches on faithfulness and on serving God versus Mammon. He answers the scoffing Pharisees by saying God knows their hearts, speaks about the law, the Kingdom and divorce, and tells the parable of the rich man and Lazarus.

l: rich man (manager's lord), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: The rich man learns his manager is wasting his possessions and demands an accounting, removing him from management. He later commends the dishonest manager for having acted wisely after the manager reduces the debtors' bills.

l: manager (dishonest manager), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: The manager is accused of wasting his lord's possessions and told he will lose his position. Unable to dig and ashamed to beg, he has debtors cut their bills (oil from a hundred to fifty batos, wheat from a hundred to eighty cors) so they will receive him into their houses, and his lord commends his wisdom.

l: mammon, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: Mammon is called unrighteous, and Jesus urges making friends by means of it so that others may receive the disciples into the eternal tents. He says no one can serve both God and Mammon.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: God is said to know the hearts of the Pharisees and to regard what is exalted among men as an abomination. Jesus states that one cannot serve both God and Mammon, and refers to the Good News of God's Kingdom being preached.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: The Pharisees, described as lovers of money, hear Jesus' teaching and scoff at him. Jesus tells them they justify themselves before men, but God knows their hearts.

l: rich man (in Lazarus parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: The rich man dresses in purple and fine linen and lives in luxury daily, while a beggar lies at his gate. After death he is buried and is tormented in Hades, where he begs Abraham to send Lazarus to cool his tongue and then to warn his brothers, but both requests are refused.

l: Lazarus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: Lazarus is a beggar covered in sores, laid at the rich man's gate, desiring crumbs from his table while dogs lick his sores. When he dies, angels carry him to Abraham's bosom, where he is comforted.

l: Abraham, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: Abraham receives Lazarus at his bosom and tells the tormented rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad. He says a great gulf prevents crossing between them and that the brothers have Moses and the prophets, and would not be persuaded even if one rose from the dead.

l: Hades, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: Hades is the place where the rich man lifts his eyes in torment after death, in anguish in flame. It is separated from Abraham and Lazarus by a great fixed gulf that no one can cross.

l: five brothers (rich man's brothers), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 16
s: The rich man's five brothers are still living in his father's house, and he asks that Lazarus be sent to testify to them so they avoid the place of torment. Abraham answers that they have Moses and the prophets to listen to.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: In Chapter 17, Jesus teaches his disciples about causing others to stumble, rebuking and forgiving a brother who sins repeatedly, and the power of faith like a mustard seed, then illustrates duty with the image of a servant. On the way to Jerusalem, he meets ten lepers who ask for mercy; he sends them to the priests and they are cleansed as they go, but only one, a Samaritan, returns to thank him and is told his faith has healed him. Asked by the Pharisees when God's Kingdom will come, Jesus says it does not come with observation and is within them. He then tells the disciples that the Son of Man must first suffer and be rejected, and that his coming will be sudden like lightning, comparable to the days of Noah and Lot, with one person taken and another left.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: Jesus warns the disciples against causing little ones to stumble, instructs them to rebuke and forgive a repentant brother, and teaches about faith and a servant's duty. He cleanses ten lepers by sending them to the priests, commends the returning Samaritan, answers the Pharisees about God's Kingdom, and describes the coming of the Son of Man, who must first suffer and be rejected.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: The disciples (called apostles in verse 5) are taught about stumbling blocks and forgiveness, and ask the Lord to increase their faith. Jesus tells them they will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man and not see it, and warns them not to follow those who say 'Look, here!' or 'Look, there!'

l: Samaritan leper (one of the ten lepers), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: The Samaritan was cleansed with the other nine as they went to show themselves to the priests. He alone turned back, glorifying God loudly and falling at Jesus' feet in thanks, and Jesus told him to get up and go, saying his faith had healed him.

l: ten lepers, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: Ten men with leprosy stood at a distance and cried out to Jesus for mercy. Told to show themselves to the priests, all ten were cleansed as they went, but only one returned to give thanks, leaving Jesus to ask where the nine were.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: Asked by the Pharisees when it would come, Jesus answered that God's Kingdom does not come with observation and that people will not say 'Look, here!' or 'Look, there!' He said that it is within them.

l: forgiveness, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: Jesus instructs that if a brother sins, he should be rebuked, and if he repents, he must be forgiven. This applies even if he sins seven times in a day and seven times returns saying 'I repent.'

l: faith, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: When the apostles ask for increased faith, Jesus says faith like a mustard seed could make a sycamore tree uproot and plant itself in the sea. He later tells the thankful Samaritan that his faith has healed him.

l: coming of the Son of Man, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 17
s: Jesus says the Son of Man will be like lightning flashing across the sky in his day, but must first suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. He compares it to the days of Noah and Lot, when people went on with ordinary life until sudden destruction, and says that on that night one person will be taken and another left.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: In Luke 18, Jesus teaches about prayer through two parables: a widow who persistently pleads with an unrighteous judge until he defends her, and a Pharisee and a tax collector who pray in the temple, with the humble tax collector going home justified. Jesus then tells his disciples to let babies and little children come to him, saying God's Kingdom belongs to such as these. A rich ruler asks how to inherit eternal life, is told to sell everything and give to the poor, and leaves very sad; Jesus remarks on how hard it is for the rich to enter the Kingdom and says what is impossible with men is possible with God. Jesus tells the twelve he will be handed over, killed, and rise on the third day, though they do not understand, and near Jericho he heals a blind man who cries out to him as son of David.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: Jesus tells parables about persistent prayer and about a Pharisee and tax collector, welcomes little children, and tells a rich ruler to sell all and follow him. He predicts to the twelve that he will be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, killed, and rise on the third day, then heals a blind man near Jericho, saying his faith has healed him.

l: unrighteous judge (parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: The judge neither fears God nor respects man and at first refuses a widow's plea. Because her continual coming bothers him and might wear him out, he decides to defend her.

l: widow (parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: The widow repeatedly comes to the judge asking him to defend her from her adversary. Her persistence eventually wins her the defense she sought.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: Jesus says God will avenge his chosen ones who cry to him day and night, and will do so quickly while exercising patience with them. Jesus also says only God is good, and that things impossible with men are possible with God. The tax collector asks him for mercy, and the healed blind man and the people praise him.

l: Pharisee (parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: The Pharisee stands apart in the temple and thanks God that he is not like other men or the tax collector, citing his fasting twice a week and his tithes. Jesus says the tax collector, not he, went home justified, because those who exalt themselves will be humbled.

l: tax collector (parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: The tax collector stands far off, will not lift his eyes, beats his chest, and asks God to be merciful to him, a sinner. Jesus says he went down to his house justified rather than the Pharisee.

l: babies and little children, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: People bring babies to Jesus to be touched, and the disciples rebuke them. Jesus summons them, tells the disciples not to hinder them, and says God's Kingdom belongs to such as these and must be received like a little child.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: Jesus says it belongs to little children and that whoever does not receive it like a little child will not enter it. He says it is very hard for the rich to enter, easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye, and that people who leave family for its sake will receive many times more in this time and eternal life to come.

l: rich ruler, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: The ruler calls Jesus good teacher and asks how to inherit eternal life, saying he has kept the commandments since youth. Told to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow Jesus, he becomes very sad because he is very rich.

l: blind man, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: A blind man begging by the road near Jericho learns Jesus is passing and cries out for mercy as son of David, continuing louder when rebuked. Jesus tells him to receive his sight, and he immediately sees, follows Jesus, and glorifies God.

l: prayer, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 18
s: Jesus teaches that people must always pray and not give up, illustrated by the persistent widow. The Pharisee's self-righteous prayer contrasts with the tax collector's humble plea for mercy, which Jesus says leads to justification.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Jesus passes through Jericho, where he sees Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, in a sycamore tree and stays at his house; Zacchaeus pledges half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution, and Jesus declares salvation has come to the house. Because he is near Jerusalem and the people expect the Kingdom immediately, Jesus tells a parable of a nobleman who gives ten servants a mina each before going away to receive a kingdom, then rewards the faithful, condemns the servant who hid his mina, and orders his enemies killed. Jesus then goes up to Jerusalem, sending two disciples to fetch a colt, and rides it down the Mount of Olives while disciples praise him as King. When the Pharisees ask him to rebuke them, he refuses, then weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its destruction. He enters the temple, drives out the sellers, and teaches daily while the chief priests, scribes, and leaders seek to destroy him but are hindered by the people's attention.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Jesus passes through Jericho, stays at Zacchaeus's house, and says he came to seek and save the lost. He tells the parable of the minas, rides a colt into the Mount of Olives descent to acclaim as King, weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its fall, drives sellers out of the temple, and teaches daily while leaders seek to destroy him.

l: Zacchaeus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector who is short, climbs a sycamore tree to see Jesus and receives him joyfully at his house despite the crowd's murmuring. He promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold restoration to anyone he wrongfully exacted from, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house because he too is a son of Abraham.

l: parable of the minas, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Jesus tells this parable because he is near Jerusalem and the people think God's Kingdom will appear immediately. It describes a nobleman who leaves to receive a kingdom, rewards servants according to their gains, takes the mina from the one who hid it, and orders his enemies who rejected his reign killed.

l: nobleman (in the parable), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: The nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom, gives ten servants ten minas to do business with, and is hated by his citizens, who send an envoy saying they don't want him to reign. On returning he rewards the first two servants with authority over ten and five cities, judges the third by his own words, gives that servant's mina to the one with ten, and commands his enemies be killed before him.

l: servants (of the nobleman), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Ten servants each receive a mina and are told to conduct business until the nobleman comes. The first gains ten minas and the second five and both are given authority over cities, while another, who hid his mina in a handkerchief out of fear, is called wicked and has it taken away.

l: Jerusalem, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem and approaches it by the Mount of Olives, where he sees the city and weeps. He says it did not know the things of its peace or the time of its visitation, and predicts enemies will surround it, dash its people to the ground, and leave no stone on another.

l: colt, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: A colt that no one has ever sat on is found tied in the village, as Jesus told two disciples it would be. When its owners ask why it is untied, the disciples say the Lord needs it, and they bring it to Jesus, put their cloaks on it, and sit him on it as people spread cloaks on the road.

l: temple, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 19
s: Jesus enters the temple and drives out those buying and selling, saying it is written that his house is a house of prayer but they have made it a den of robbers. He teaches there daily, while the chief priests, scribes, and leading men seek to destroy him but cannot, because all the people hang on his words.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: In the temple, Jesus is questioned by the priests, scribes and elders about his authority, and he counters by asking whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men; they refuse to answer, so he refuses to answer them. He then tells the parable of a man who rented his vineyard to farmers who beat his servants and killed his beloved son, and he cites the rejected stone that became the cornerstone, which the leaders recognize as aimed at them. Spies sent by the leaders ask whether taxes should be paid to Caesar, and Jesus answers by having them identify Caesar's image on a denarius and telling them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a case of seven brothers who each married one woman, and Jesus replies that those who attain the resurrection neither marry nor die and that God is God of the living. He then asks how the Christ can be David's son when David calls him Lord, and warns his disciples against scribes who seek honor and devour widows' houses.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus teaches in the temple and silences the priests, scribes and elders by asking about John's baptism, then tells the vineyard parable against them. He answers the question about Caesar's taxes and the Sadducees' resurrection question, asks how the Christ can be David's son, and warns his disciples against the scribes.

l: priests and scribes, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: The priests and scribes, with the elders, challenge Jesus' authority but cannot answer his question about John's baptism for fear of the people. They seek to lay hands on him after the parable, send spies to trap him, and are warned by Jesus of greater condemnation for seeking honor and devouring widows' houses.

l: baptism of repentance, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus asks whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men. The leaders reason that either answer would hurt them, since the people are persuaded John was a prophet, and they say they don't know.

l: authority of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: The priests, scribes and elders ask by what authority Jesus does these things and who gave it to him. Jesus answers with a counter-question and then declines to tell them, since they would not answer his.

l: vineyard parable, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus tells the people of a man who rented a vineyard to farmers, who beat and sent away three servants and killed the owner's son. The owner will destroy the farmers and give the vineyard to others, and the leaders perceive it was spoken against them.

l: man (owner of the vineyard), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: In the parable, the man plants a vineyard, rents it to farmers and goes to another country for a long time. He sends three servants to collect his share of the fruit and then his beloved son, and he will come and destroy the farmers and give the vineyard to others.

l: farmers, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: In the parable, the farmers beat and shamefully treat the owner's servants and send them away empty or wounded. They kill the heir to gain the inheritance, and they are told the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others.

l: son (beloved son of the vineyard owner), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: The owner sends his beloved son in hope that the farmers will respect him. The farmers recognize him as the heir, throw him out of the vineyard and kill him.

l: Caesar, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Caesar's image and inscription are on the denarius that Jesus has the spies show him. Jesus says to give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

l: taxes to Caesar, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: The spies flatter Jesus and ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, hoping to trap him before the governor. He has them name Caesar's image on a denarius and tells them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, and they are silenced.

l: God, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus says to give to God the things that are God's. He describes those of the resurrection as children of God and says God, called by Moses the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, is God of the living, for all are alive to him.

l: Sadducees, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask Jesus about a woman who married seven brothers in turn and whose wife she will be in the resurrection. Jesus answers that the resurrected neither marry nor die and that God is God of the living.

l: resurrection, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus says those considered worthy of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage and cannot die any more, being like the angels and children of God. He cites Moses at the bush as showing that the dead are raised.

l: David, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus cites David's words in the book of Psalms, 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.' He asks how the Christ can be David's son when David calls him Lord.

l: Christ, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 20
s: Jesus asks why people say the Christ is David's son, since David himself calls him Lord in the Psalms. The question of how he can be both is left posed in this unit.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: In Chapter 21, Jesus observes rich people giving gifts to the treasury and praises a poor widow who gave two small coins, all she had to live on. When some remark on the temple's beautiful stones, he predicts that not one stone will be left on another, and his listeners ask when this will happen and what the sign will be. Jesus warns them not to be led astray by false claimants, describes wars, earthquakes, famines, plagues, and persecution of his followers, and says Jerusalem will be surrounded by armies, desolated, and trampled by the Gentiles. He foretells signs in the sun, moon, and stars, the coming of the Son of Man in a cloud with power and glory, and teaches the fig tree parable, urging watchfulness and prayer. The chapter closes with Jesus teaching in the temple by day, lodging on Olivet at night, and the people coming early to hear him.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Jesus commends a poor widow's offering and predicts the temple's total destruction when asked about it. He answers his listeners' questions about signs, warning against deceivers, foretelling persecution, the fall of Jerusalem, and the coming of the Son of Man, and urges watchfulness. He teaches daily in the temple and spends nights on the mountain called Olivet.

l: poor widow, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: A poor widow casts two small brass coins into the treasury. Jesus says she put in more than all the rich givers, because they gave from their abundance while she gave all she had to live on.

l: temple, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: The temple is noted by some for its beautiful stones and gifts, and Jesus says days will come when not one stone is left on another that is not thrown down. It is also where Jesus teaches every day and where all the people come early in the morning to hear him.

l: Jerusalem, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Jesus says Jerusalem will be surrounded by armies, signaling that its desolation is at hand. Its people will fall by the sword and be led captive into all nations, and the city will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

l: Son of Man, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Jesus says people will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. He tells his listeners to pray to be counted worthy to stand before the Son of Man.

l: disciples (Jesus' listeners), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Some of Jesus' listeners talk about the temple's decoration, then ask when the destruction will come and what the sign will be. Jesus warns them not to be led astray or terrified, tells them not to prepare their defense beforehand, promises not a hair of their heads will perish, and urges endurance and watchfulness.

l: persecution of followers, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Jesus foretells that before the other events, his followers will be seized, persecuted, delivered to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors for his name's sake. They will be betrayed by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, some will be put to death, and all will hate them. It will serve as a testimony, he will give them a mouth and wisdom no adversary can withstand, and by endurance they will win their lives.

l: destruction of Jerusalem (Jesus' prophecy), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Jesus predicts that when Jerusalem is surrounded by armies its desolation is near, and he tells those in Judea to flee to the mountains. He calls these days of vengeance fulfilling what is written, with great distress, wrath on the people, death by the sword, and captivity among the nations.

l: signs in the heavens and on earth, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 21
s: Jesus describes wars, nations rising against nations, great earthquakes, famines, plagues, terrors, and great signs from heaven. He adds signs in the sun, moon, and stars, anxiety among nations over the roaring sea, and people fainting for fear as the powers of the heavens are shaken. He says that when these begin, his followers should lift their heads because their redemption is near, and that they signal God's Kingdom is near, like budding fig trees signal summer.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: As the Passover approaches, the chief priests and scribes seek to kill Jesus, and Satan enters Judas Iscariot, who agrees with them to betray Jesus for money. Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover, then shares the meal with the twelve apostles, giving the bread and cup as his body and the new covenant in his blood, and announcing a betrayer at the table. The apostles dispute who is greatest, and Jesus teaches service and confers a kingdom on them, then warns Peter that he will deny him three times. On the Mount of Olives Jesus prays in agony, Judas leads a crowd to arrest him, and Jesus heals the ear of the high priest's servant. Peter denies Jesus three times in the high priest's courtyard and weeps when the rooster crows, while the elders mock Jesus and question him, and he affirms that he is the Son of God.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover, shares it with the twelve apostles, and gives the bread and cup as his body and the new covenant in his blood. He teaches that the greatest must serve, predicts Peter's denial, prays in agony on the Mount of Olives, heals the servant's ear, and is arrested. Before the council he says the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God and affirms that he is the Son of God.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: Peter is sent with John to prepare the Passover and tells Jesus he is ready to go to prison and death with him. Jesus warns that Satan sought to sift the apostles, says he prayed for Peter's faith, and predicts that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows. Peter follows the arrested Jesus at a distance, denies knowing him three times, and weeps bitterly when the rooster crows and Jesus looks at him.

l: Judas Iscariot, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: Satan enters Judas, who is counted among the twelve, and he arranges with the chief priests and captains to deliver Jesus to them for money in the absence of the crowd. Jesus says his betrayer's hand is with him on the table. Judas later leads the crowd to Jesus and approaches to kiss him, and Jesus asks if he betrays the Son of Man with a kiss.

l: chief priests, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: The chief priests, with the scribes, seek a way to kill Jesus because they fear the people, and they gladly agree to give Judas money. Chief priests, temple captains, and elders come against Jesus with swords and clubs, and Jesus tells them it is their hour and the power of darkness. Chief priests and scribes later gather with the elders in council, question Jesus, and declare they need no more witness after hearing him say he is the Son of God.

l: the twelve, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: Jesus sits down with the twelve apostles at the Passover meal, and they receive the cup and bread. They question which of them will betray him and dispute over who is greatest, and Jesus promises them a kingdom and thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. On the Mount of Olives they sleep from grief while Jesus prays, and one of the twelve, Judas, leads the arresting crowd.

l: Passover, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: The feast of unleavened bread, called the Passover, is approaching as the chief priests plot against Jesus. Jesus directs Peter and John to a large furnished upper room to prepare it. He says he has earnestly desired to eat this Passover with the apostles before he suffers and will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in God's Kingdom.

l: Last Supper, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: At the meal Jesus shares a cup, then breaks bread and gives it as his body given for the apostles, telling them to do this in memory of him. After supper he gives the cup as the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them. During the meal he announces that his betrayer is at the table, the apostles dispute who is greatest, and he warns Peter of denial.

l: prayer in Gethsemane, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: On the Mount of Olives Jesus tells the disciples to pray not to enter temptation, withdraws about a stone's throw, kneels, and asks the Father to remove the cup while submitting to his will. An angel from heaven strengthens him, and in agony his sweat becomes like great drops of blood. He returns to find the disciples sleeping from grief and tells them to rise and pray.

l: arrest of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: While Jesus is still speaking, a crowd led by Judas arrives, and Judas approaches to kiss him. One of the disciples strikes the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear, but Jesus heals it and tells the chief priests, captains, and elders that this is their hour and the power of darkness. They seize him and bring him to the high priest's house, where the men holding him mock and beat him.

l: Peter's denial, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 22
s: In the courtyard of the high priest's house, a servant girl, then another person, then a third after about an hour say Peter was with Jesus. Peter denies it each time, saying he does not know him, is not one of them, and does not know what they mean. A rooster crows immediately after the third denial, Jesus looks at him, Peter remembers the prediction, and he goes out and weeps bitterly.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Jesus is brought before Pilate by the whole company of accusers, who charge him with perverting the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be Christ, a king. Pilate finds no basis for a charge and sends him to Herod, who mocks him and returns him; Pilate then yields to the crowd and the chief priests, releasing Barabbas and delivering Jesus to their will. Jesus is led out with Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross, warns the mourning daughters of Jerusalem, and is crucified at The Skull between two criminals, one of whom rebukes the other and is promised Paradise. Jesus dies after darkness covers the land and the temple veil is torn, and the centurion calls him righteous. Joseph of Arimathaea, a council member who had not consented to the others' deed, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in a rock-cut tomb, and the women from Galilee watch and prepare spices before resting on the Sabbath.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Jesus is accused before Pilate, answers 'So you say' to the question whether he is King of the Jews, and stays silent before Herod. He is condemned at the crowd's demand, crucified, and prays 'Father, forgive them.' He promises the repentant criminal Paradise, commits his spirit to the Father, and dies; his body is laid in a tomb.

l: Pilate, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Pilate questions Jesus, three times declares he finds no basis for a charge or capital crime, and sends him to Herod. Despite offering to chastise and release him, he yields to the loud voices, releases Barabbas, and delivers Jesus to the crowd's will. He also becomes friends with Herod that day and grants Joseph's request for the body.

l: Herod, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Herod, in Jerusalem at the time, is glad to see Jesus, having long wanted to see a miracle from him. He questions him at length without answer, mocks him with his soldiers, dresses him in luxurious clothing, and sends him back to Pilate. He and Pilate, formerly enemies, become friends that day.

l: chief priests, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: The chief priests, with the scribes, vehemently accuse Jesus before Herod and press the charges before Pilate. Their voices, with the crowd's, prevail in securing Jesus' crucifixion, and the rulers scoff at him on the cross.

l: Barabbas, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Barabbas is described as a prisoner thrown into prison for a revolt in the city and for murder. The crowd demands his release instead of Jesus, and Pilate releases him.

l: criminal (repentant), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: One of two criminals crucified with Jesus rebukes the other for insulting Jesus, saying they receive their just reward while Jesus has done nothing wrong. He asks Jesus to remember him in his Kingdom and is told, 'today you will be with me in Paradise.'

l: Joseph of Arimathaea, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Joseph is introduced as a good and righteous member of the council from Arimathaea who was waiting for God's Kingdom and had not consented to the council's counsel and deed. He asks Pilate for Jesus' body, takes it down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in an unused rock-cut tomb.

l: The Skull, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: The Skull is the place where Jesus is led and crucified with two criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

l: tomb, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: The tomb is cut in stone and had never held anyone before. Joseph lays Jesus' wrapped body there on the day of Preparation, and the women from Galilee see it and how the body was placed.

l: Jesus' crucifixion and suffering, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Jesus is crucified at The Skull between two criminals, with soldiers dividing his garments by lot and an inscription reading 'THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.' He is mocked by rulers, soldiers, and one criminal; from the sixth to ninth hour darkness covers the land, the temple veil tears, and he dies. The centurion glorifies God, and the crowds return home beating their chests.

l: trial of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 23
s: Jesus is tried before Pilate, sent to Herod, and returned, with Pilate finding no basis for a charge. The crowd and chief priests demand crucifixion and the release of Barabbas, and Pilate decrees that their request be done.

l: The Gospel According to Luke, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Luke 24 begins on the first day of the week, when Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women find Jesus' tomb empty and hear two men in dazzling clothing say he is risen. The apostles dismiss their report as nonsense, though Peter runs to the tomb and sees only the linen strips. That day Jesus joins two disciples, one named Cleopas, on the road to Emmaus, explains the Scriptures about himself, and is recognized by them in the breaking of the bread. They return to Jerusalem, where Jesus appears among the eleven and others, shows his hands and feet, eats broiled fish, opens their minds to the Scriptures, and commissions them as witnesses. He then leads them to Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven, and they return to Jerusalem worshiping with great joy.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Jesus joins two disciples on the road to Emmaus without being recognized, explains from Moses and all the prophets the things concerning himself, and is recognized when he breaks bread. He then appears to the gathered disciples in Jerusalem, shows his hands and feet, eats fish and honeycomb, opens their minds to understand the Scriptures, and tells them to wait for the promise of the Father. He blesses them at Bethany and is carried up into heaven.

l: women (Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: The women come to the tomb at early dawn with spices, find the stone rolled away and the body missing, and are told by two men that Jesus is risen. They remember his words, return and tell the eleven and all the rest, but the apostles think their words nonsense and do not believe them.

l: tomb (Jesus' tomb), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: The tomb is found with its stone rolled away and Jesus' body not inside. Peter later runs there, stoops, and sees only the strips of linen lying by themselves; other disciples also go and find it as the women said.

l: two men (angels at the tomb), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Two men in dazzling clothing stand by the women at the tomb and terrify them. They ask why the women seek the living among the dead, announce that Jesus is risen, and remind them of what he said in Galilee about being delivered up, crucified, and rising on the third day. The Emmaus disciples later describe them as a vision of angels who said he was alive.

l: Cleopas, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Cleopas is one of two disciples walking to Emmaus. He answers the unrecognized Jesus by asking if he is the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn't know what has happened, and he recounts Jesus' death, their lost hope of redemption, and the women's report of the empty tomb.

l: two disciples (on the road to Emmaus), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Two disciples walk to Emmaus that day, talking about the events, and their eyes are kept from recognizing Jesus when he joins them. They urge him to stay, recognize him at the breaking of the bread, and say their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures. They return at once to Jerusalem and tell the eleven what happened on the way.

l: Emmaus, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Emmaus is a village sixty stadia from Jerusalem, toward which two disciples travel on the day of the resurrection. Jesus goes in to stay with them there, and they recognize him at the table before he vanishes from their sight.

l: Jerusalem, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Jerusalem is where the disciples gather and receive the women's report, and where the Emmaus disciples return to find the eleven. Jesus appears there, says repentance and remission of sins will be preached to all nations beginning at Jerusalem, and tells the disciples to wait in the city until clothed with power from on high. They return there with great joy after his ascension and are continually in the temple.

l: Scriptures, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: Jesus explains to the Emmaus disciples, beginning from Moses and all the prophets, the things concerning himself, and says the Christ had to suffer and enter his glory. He later says all that is written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms about him must be fulfilled, and he opens the disciples' minds to understand them.

l: breaking of the bread (meal at Emmaus), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: At the table in Emmaus, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to the two disciples. Their eyes are opened and they recognize him, and then he vanishes. They later relate that he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.

l: Jesus' resurrection, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: The two men announce that Jesus is risen, and the report is confirmed when Jesus appears to Simon, to the Emmaus disciples, and to the gathered group. He shows his hands and feet, says a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones, and eats in front of them. He says it was written that the Christ would suffer and rise from the dead the third day.

l: Jesus' ascension, The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: After blessing the disciples at Bethany with lifted hands, Jesus withdraws from them and is carried up into heaven. The disciples worship him and return to Jerusalem with great joy.

l: disciples (the eleven and companions in Jerusalem), The Gospel According to Luke, Chapter 24
s: The eleven and others first disbelieve the women's report, then gather and say the Lord is risen and has appeared to Simon. When Jesus appears, they are terrified and think he is a spirit, but he shows them his hands and feet and eats before them. He opens their minds, names them witnesses, tells them to wait for power from on high, and after his ascension they worship him and continually praise God in the temple.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: The narrator addresses Theophilus and recalls that his first book covered what Jesus began to do and teach. Over forty days after his suffering Jesus appeared to the apostles he had chosen, spoke about God's Kingdom, and told them to wait in Jerusalem for baptism in the Holy Spirit; he then promised them power to be witnesses to the uttermost parts of the earth and was taken up in a cloud while two men in white told them he would return in the same way. The apostles went back to Jerusalem, gathered in the upper room with the women, Mary, and Jesus' brothers, and prayed. Peter, standing among about one hundred twenty disciples, explained that Judas, who guided those who took Jesus, had fallen and died, and that a replacement witness of the resurrection was needed. Two men, Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias, were put forward, and after prayer the lot fell on Matthias, who was counted with the eleven apostles.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Jesus showed himself alive to the apostles after he suffered, by many proofs over forty days, speaking about God's Kingdom. He told them to wait in Jerusalem for the Father's promise, said they would receive power and be witnesses, and was taken up as a cloud received him out of sight. Two men in white said he would come back in the same way he went.

l: Holy Spirit, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Jesus gave commandment to the apostles through the Holy Spirit, and promised that they would be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days later. He said they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them, and Peter said the Holy Spirit had spoken by David's mouth about Judas.

l: apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: The apostles, whom Jesus had chosen, were shown him alive over forty days and were told to wait in Jerusalem and to be his witnesses to the uttermost parts of the earth. After watching him taken up, they returned to Jerusalem, stayed in the upper room, and continued in prayer. The eleven are named, and Matthias was counted with them after the lot fell on him.

l: Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Jesus commanded the apostles not to depart from Jerusalem but to wait there for the Father's promise, and it is the first place of their witness. They returned there from the Mount of Olives, a Sabbath day's journey away, and gathered in the upper room. Everyone living in Jerusalem came to know that Judas's field was called Akeldama, the field of blood.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Peter is listed first among the eleven in the upper room. He stood among about one hundred twenty disciples and said that Scripture about Judas had to be fulfilled. He declared that one of the men who had accompanied them from John's baptism to the ascension must become a witness of the resurrection.

l: Judas, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Judas was guide to those who took Jesus, though he was counted with the apostles and received a portion in their ministry. He obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness, fell headlong, and his body burst open. The apostles prayed that his place might be taken by another, since he fell away to go to his own place.

l: Matthias, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Matthias was one of two men put forward to replace Judas, the other being Joseph called Barsabbas, also called Justus. When lots were drawn, the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles.

l: Ascension of Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: After speaking to the apostles, Jesus was taken up as they were looking, and a cloud received him out of their sight. While they gazed into the sky, two men in white clothing told them, 'You men of Galilee,' that Jesus would come back in the same way they saw him go. The apostles then returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet.

l: selection of Judas's replacement, The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles / Chapter 1
s: Peter said one of the men who had accompanied them from John's baptism until Jesus was received up must become a witness of the resurrection in Judas's place, citing Psalms. They put forward Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias, prayed that the Lord who knows all hearts would show his choice, and drew lots. The lot fell on Matthias, who was counted with the eleven apostles.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: On the day of Pentecost, the believers gathered in one place are filled with the Holy Spirit after a sound like a rushing wind and tongues like fire appear, and they begin speaking in other languages. Jews from many nations in Jerusalem hear them in their own languages; some are amazed while others mock them as drunk on new wine. Peter, standing with the eleven, answers that this fulfills Joel's prophecy and proclaims that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified by lawless men, was raised by God, exalted, and made both Lord and Christ. Cut to the heart, the listeners ask what to do, and Peter tells them to repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins, after which about three thousand are added. The believers then devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayer, and sharing of goods, and the Lord adds to their number daily.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Peter stands up with the eleven, lifts his voice, and answers the mockers by explaining that the believers are not drunk but are fulfilling Joel's prophecy. He preaches Jesus' death and resurrection, citing David, and tells the cut-to-the-heart crowd to repent and be baptized, urging them to save themselves from this crooked generation.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Jesus is described as a man approved by God through mighty works, wonders, and signs, delivered up by God's counsel and crucified by lawless men. God raised him from death, exalted him to his right hand, and made him both Lord and Christ; baptism is to be in his name.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: God is said to have poured out his Spirit as promised through Joel, approved Jesus by wonders, and raised him from death because death could not hold him. He exalted Jesus to his right hand, made him Lord and Christ, and calls to himself those to whom the promise extends.

l: Holy Spirit, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: The Holy Spirit fills all the gathered believers, who speak in other languages as the Spirit gives them ability. Peter explains that Jesus, having received the promise of the Spirit from the Father, has poured it out, and that repentant, baptized people will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

l: disciples (believers gathered at Pentecost), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: The believers are together with one accord in one place when tongues like fire rest on each of them and they are all filled with the Holy Spirit and speak in other languages. Some onlookers mock them as full of new wine, but they are later joined by about three thousand who are baptized.

l: multitude (Jews in Jerusalem), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Devout Jews from every nation under the sky gather, bewildered and amazed to hear the believers speaking in their own native languages about the mighty works of God. Some are perplexed and others mock; after Peter's sermon they are cut to the heart and ask what to do, and about three thousand receive his word and are baptized.

l: Pentecost, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Pentecost is the day on which the believers are gathered in one place when the sound like a mighty wind comes and the Holy Spirit is poured out. It is also the day on which about three thousand souls are added to the believers.

l: speaking in other languages, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Upon being filled with the Spirit, the believers speak in other languages, and people from many nations each hear them in their own native language declaring God's mighty works. The phenomenon causes amazement and perplexity in some and mockery in others, and Peter explains it as the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy.

l: Peter's Pentecost sermon, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Peter addresses the men of Judea and Israel, declaring that the believers are not drunk but fulfilling Joel's prophecy, and that Jesus, crucified by lawless men, was raised by God as David foretold. He concludes that God has made this Jesus both Lord and Christ, which cuts the hearers to the heart.

l: resurrection of Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Peter says God raised Jesus up, freeing him from the agony of death because death could not hold him. He argues that David, who died and whose tomb remains, foretold this when he spoke of the Holy One not being left in Hades or seeing decay, and that the apostles are all witnesses.

l: baptism and repentance, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: Asked what to do, Peter tells every one to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins and receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, with the promise extending to their children and to all who are far off. Those who gladly receive his word are baptized, about three thousand that day.

l: early church community life, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 2
s: The new believers continue steadfastly in the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer, and fear comes on every soul as wonders and signs are done through the apostles. They hold all things in common, sell possessions to meet needs, meet daily in the temple and at home with gladness, praise God, and have favor with all the people while the Lord adds those being saved.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer, where a man lame from birth is laid daily at the Beautiful gate to beg. Peter tells him he has no silver or gold, and in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth commands him to get up and walk; he takes the man's right hand, and the man is healed and enters the temple leaping and praising God. The amazed people run together to them at Solomon's porch, and Peter tells them the healing came by faith in Jesus' name, not by the apostles' own power. He says God glorified his Servant Jesus, whom the people delivered up and denied, and whom God raised from the dead. Peter calls them to repent and turn again so their sins may be blotted out and times of refreshing may come, citing Moses and the prophets, and says God sent Jesus first to them to bless them by turning each from wickedness.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: Peter goes up to the temple with John, tells the lame man he has no silver or gold, and commands him in Jesus' name to get up and walk, raising him by the right hand. He then addresses the astonished crowd, denying that the healing came from his own power or godliness, accusing them of denying Jesus, and calling them to repent.

l: John, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: John goes up to the temple with Peter at the ninth hour and is told by Peter, together with him, to be looked at by the lame man. The healed man holds on to John and Peter as the people run together to them at Solomon's porch.

l: lame man (healed by Peter and John), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: The man, lame from his mother's womb, is carried daily to the temple door called Beautiful to ask for gifts for the needy. After Peter raises him in Jesus' name, his feet and ankle bones receive strength, and he enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, and the people recognize him as the one who used to sit begging.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: His name is the one in which Peter commands the lame man to walk, and Peter says faith in his name made the man strong. Peter calls him God's glorified Servant, the Holy and Righteous One and Prince of life, whom the people delivered up and denied before Pilate and killed, but whom God raised from the dead. Heaven must receive him until the times of restoration, and God sent him first to the people to bless them.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: God is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who glorified his Servant Jesus and raised him from the dead. He announced through all his prophets that Christ would suffer, will send Christ Jesus again, and made a covenant with the fathers promising that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham's offspring.

l: temple, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: The temple is the place Peter and John go to at the hour of prayer, with its door called Beautiful where the lame man begs daily. The healed man enters it walking and praising God, and the people gather in Solomon's porch.

l: people (in the temple), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: The people see the healed man walking and praising God, recognize him as the former beggar, and are filled with wonder and amazement. They run together to Peter and John at Solomon's porch, where Peter rebukes them for delivering up and denying Jesus, says they acted in ignorance, and calls them children of the prophets and of the covenant.

l: healing of the lame man, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: The man is healed when Peter commands him in Jesus' name to walk and takes his right hand, and his feet and ankle bones immediately gain strength. Peter explains it was not by the apostles' own power or godliness but by faith in Jesus' name, which gave the man perfect soundness before everyone.

l: repentance and restoration, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 3
s: Peter urges the people to repent and turn again so that their sins may be blotted out and times of refreshing may come from the Lord's presence. He says God may send Christ Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things spoken by the prophets, and warns through Moses that every soul that will not listen to the promised prophet will be utterly destroyed.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: Peter and John, while speaking to the people, are seized by the priests, the captain of the temple, and the Sadducees, who are upset that they proclaim the resurrection in Jesus, and are held overnight while about five thousand men believe. The next morning the rulers, elders, and scribes, including Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, and Alexander, question them, and Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says the crippled man was healed in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth and that there is salvation in no other name. Unable to deny the miracle, the council threatens Peter and John and orders them not to speak in Jesus' name, but they answer that they cannot help telling what they saw and heard, and are released. The believers pray to God, quoting David, and ask for boldness; the place is shaken and they are filled with the Holy Spirit. The chapter ends with the believers sharing all possessions, the apostles testifying to the resurrection, and Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, selling a field and laying the money at the apostles' feet.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, tells the rulers and elders that the crippled man was healed in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised. He declares Jesus the rejected stone that became the head of the corner and says there is salvation in no other name.

l: John, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: John is arrested with Peter while speaking to the people and is held overnight. A different John is also named among those present with the high priest's relatives at the council.

l: Peter and John, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: Peter and John are seized, held until morning, and questioned by the council. The council marvels at their boldness, perceives them as unlearned and ignorant men, and recognizes that they had been with Jesus. After being threatened and commanded not to speak in Jesus' name, they answer that they cannot help telling what they saw and heard, and they are released.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: Jesus is the name in which the crippled man was healed, and Peter says he was crucified by the rulers but raised by God. He is called the stone rejected by the builders that became the head of the corner, and the only name under heaven by which people must be saved. The believers' prayer calls him God's holy Servant, whom God anointed and against whom Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel gathered.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: God raised Jesus from the dead, according to Peter, and is addressed in the believers' prayer as Lord who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all in them. The prayer says he spoke through David and that his hand and counsel foreordained what happened to Jesus. He answers the prayer by shaking the place and filling the believers with the Holy Spirit.

l: rulers, elders and scribes (council), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: The rulers, elders, and scribes gather in Jerusalem the next morning and question Peter and John about the power or name behind the healing. Unable to deny the notable miracle, they confer privately, decide to threaten the apostles to stop the matter spreading, and command them not to speak or teach in Jesus' name. They release them, finding no way to punish them because of the people.

l: believers, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: Many who heard the word believe, bringing the number of men to about five thousand. After Peter and John report, they pray together, are filled with the Holy Spirit, and speak God's word boldly. They are of one heart and soul and hold all things in common.

l: lame man (healed by Peter and John), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: The healed man stands before the council whole, and the rulers can say nothing against it. He is said to be more than forty years old.

l: healing of the lame man, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: The healing of the crippled man is called a good deed and a notable miracle, plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and the council admits it cannot be denied. Peter attributes it to the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and everyone glorifies God for it.

l: resurrection, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: The proclamation of the resurrection from the dead in Jesus is what upsets the priests, the temple captain, and the Sadducees. Peter says God raised Jesus from the dead, and the apostles give testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus with great power.

l: apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: The apostles testify to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus with great power, and great grace is on them all. Believers who sell lands or houses lay the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and distribution is made to each according to need.

l: Barnabas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: Joses, called Barnabas by the apostles, meaning Son of Encouragement, is introduced as a Levite and a man of Cyprus by race. He sells a field he owns and lays the money at the apostles' feet.

l: shared possessions, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: None of the believers claims his possessions as his own, and they have all things in common. Owners of lands or houses sell them and lay the proceeds at the apostles' feet, so that no one lacks and distribution is made according to need.

l: prayer of the believers, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: After hearing the council's threats, the believers lift their voice to God with one accord, address him as creator, and quote David's words about the nations and rulers raging against the Lord and his Christ. They apply this to Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and Israel against Jesus, and ask for boldness and for signs and wonders through Jesus' name. The place is shaken and they are all filled with the Holy Spirit.

l: interrogation of Peter and John, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 4
s: The council stands Peter and John in the middle and asks by what power or name they did this. Peter answers that it was in Jesus' name, after which the council confers, commands them not to speak or teach in Jesus' name, and threatens them further. Peter and John say they must listen to God rather than the council, and they are let go.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell a possession and keep back part of the price while laying the rest at the apostles' feet; Peter confronts each of them, and both fall dead and are buried by the young men, bringing great fear on the assembly. Signs and wonders follow through the apostles, believers multiply, and the sick are healed, even by Peter's shadow. The high priest and the Sadducees, jealous, imprison the apostles, but an angel of the Lord frees them at night and sends them to teach in the temple. Brought before the council, Peter and the apostles say they must obey God rather than men and witness to Jesus; the council wants to kill them until Gamaliel advises leaving them alone, so they are beaten, commanded not to speak in Jesus' name, and released. The apostles leave rejoicing and keep teaching Jesus as the Christ every day.

l: Ananias, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Ananias sold a possession, kept back part of the price, and laid the remainder at the apostles' feet. Peter told him he had lied to God, not to men, and Ananias fell down and died upon hearing this. The young men wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.

l: Sapphira, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Sapphira, aware of her husband's scheme, came in about three hours later not knowing what had happened and affirmed that the land was sold for "so much." Peter asked how they had agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord, and she fell dead at his feet. The young men buried her by her husband.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Peter confronted Ananias and Sapphira over keeping back part of the price, and each died after his words. Sick people were laid in the streets so that his shadow might overshadow them. Before the council he declared that they must obey God rather than men, and he testified that God raised up Jesus.

l: apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: The apostles received the gift at their feet, did many signs and wonders among the people, and gathered with one accord in Solomon's porch. They were jailed by the high priest, freed by an angel, and told to teach in the temple, which they did at daybreak. After being beaten and commanded not to speak in Jesus' name, they left rejoicing and continued teaching and preaching Jesus every day.

l: possession (Ananias and Sapphira's land), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: The land was sold by Ananias and Sapphira, who kept back part of the price and laid only a part at the apostles' feet. Peter noted that while they kept it, it remained their own, and after it was sold the price was in their power.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Peter says that Ananias lied to God, not to men, and that Sapphira and Ananias tempted the Spirit of the Lord. God is said to have raised up Jesus and exalted him with his right hand as Prince and Savior to give repentance and remission of sins. Gamaliel warns that if the apostles' work is of God it cannot be overthrown, and the apostles say they must obey God rather than men.

l: deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Ananias fell dead after Peter's words, and about three hours later Sapphira fell dead at Peter's feet after confirming the same account. Both were carried out and buried by the young men. Great fear came on the whole assembly and on all who heard of it.

l: high priest and chief priests, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: The high priest, with the Sadducees, was filled with jealousy and had the apostles put in public custody. After they vanished from the prison, he was perplexed, had them brought without violence to the council, and accused them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and intending to bring this man's blood on them. He and the council were cut to the heart and determined to kill them until Gamaliel spoke.

l: angel of the Lord, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: An angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night and brought the apostles out. He told them to go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.

l: rulers, elders and scribes (council), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: The council was called together by the high priest with all the senate of Israel, and sent to the prison for the apostles, who were not found there. It heard Peter's answer and was determined to kill them, but agreed with Gamaliel's counsel. It summoned the apostles, beat them, commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Peter says that God raised up Jesus, whom the council killed by hanging him on a tree, and exalted him as Prince and Savior to give repentance and remission of sins. The council commanded the apostles not to speak in his name, but the apostles rejoiced to suffer dishonor for it and kept teaching and preaching him as the Christ.

l: Gamaliel, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: Gamaliel, a Pharisee and teacher of the law honored by all the people, stood in the council and had the apostles put out for a little while. He cited Theudas and Judas of Galilee, whose movements came to nothing after they perished, and urged leaving the apostles alone, since a work of God could not be overthrown. The council agreed with him.

l: beating and release of the apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 5
s: After agreeing with Gamaliel, the council summoned the apostles, beat them, commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. The apostles departed rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus' name, and they never stopped teaching and preaching in the temple and at home.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: As the number of disciples grows, the Hellenists complain that their widows are neglected in the daily service by the Hebrews. The twelve gather the disciples and have them choose seven men to oversee the work, so the twelve can keep to prayer and the ministry of the word. The multitude chooses Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, and the apostles pray and lay hands on them. The word of God spreads and many priests become obedient to the faith. Stephen performs wonders and signs, is disputed by men from several synagogues, and is seized after they induce men to accuse him of blasphemy; false witnesses accuse him before the council, whose members see his face like that of an angel.

l: Stephen, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: Stephen, described as full of faith and the Holy Spirit, is chosen as one of the seven men and is set before the apostles, who pray and lay hands on him. Full of faith and power, he performs great wonders and signs among the people, and his opponents cannot withstand his wisdom and the Spirit by which he speaks. He is seized, brought before the council, and accused of blasphemy against Moses, God, the holy place and the law, yet the council sees his face like the face of an angel.

l: apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: The twelve summon the multitude of disciples and say it is not appropriate for them to forsake the word of God to serve tables. They direct the disciples to select seven men to appoint over the business, while they continue in prayer and the ministry of the word. They pray and lay hands on the seven chosen.

l: the Way (disciples of the Lord), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: The disciples are multiplying in number, and the whole multitude is pleased with the twelve's proposal and chooses the seven men. Their number greatly multiplies in Jerusalem, and a great company of priests becomes obedient to the faith.

l: Hellenists, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: The Hellenists raise a complaint against the Hebrews because their widows are neglected in the daily service.

l: Hebrews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: The Hebrews are the subject of the Hellenists' complaint that the Hellenist widows are neglected in the daily service.

l: seven men, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: The seven men, to be of good report and full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, are chosen by the multitude to oversee the daily service: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. They are set before the apostles, who pray and lay hands on them.

l: synagogue disputers, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: Men of the synagogue called The Libertines, and of the Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and those of Cilicia and Asia, dispute with Stephen but cannot withstand his wisdom and Spirit. They secretly induce men to claim Stephen spoke blasphemy, stir up the people, elders, and scribes, and seize him and bring him to the council.

l: false witnesses, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: False witnesses are set up before the council and claim Stephen never stops speaking blasphemous words against the holy place and the law. They say they heard him declare that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs delivered by Moses.

l: council, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 6
s: The council receives Stephen after he is seized and hears the false witnesses accuse him. All who sit in it fasten their eyes on him and see his face like the face of an angel.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Answering the high priest's question, Stephen recounts Israel's history: God's call and promise to Abraham, Joseph being sold by his brothers and rising in Egypt, the family's move to Egypt, and the oppression there. He describes Moses, who was rejected by his own people, then sent by God from the burning bush to deliver them, yet the fathers rebelled by making a calf and serving other gods. Stephen notes the tabernacle, Solomon's house, and says the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands. He then accuses his hearers of being stiff-necked, of resisting the Holy Spirit, and of betraying and murdering the Righteous One. Enraged when he says he sees Jesus standing at God's right hand, they drive him out of the city and stone him, and he dies praying for them while Saul looks on.

l: Stephen, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Stephen answers the high priest with a long review of Israel's history, then accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and killing the Righteous One. Full of the Holy Spirit, he sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand, and is stoned. He calls on the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and asks that the sin not be held against his killers before he falls asleep.

l: Abraham, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Abraham was called by God in Mesopotamia to leave his land and relatives, and lived in Haran before moving into the promised land, where he received no inheritance, not even a foot of ground. God promised the land to him and his offspring when he had no child, and gave him the covenant of circumcision. He became father of Isaac and bought a tomb at Shechem from the children of Hamor.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: God appears to Abraham, promises the land, foretells four hundred years of bondage and judgment on the oppressing nation, and is with Joseph in Egypt. He appears to Moses at the bush, sends him to deliver his people, and gives them up to serve the army of the sky after the calf. Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, since heaven is his throne and earth his footstool.

l: Moses, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Moses is born in Egypt, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, instructed in Egyptian wisdom, and is mighty in words and works. At forty he defends an oppressed Israelite by striking an Egyptian, is rejected by his brothers, and flees to Midian, where he fathers two sons. After forty more years God appears to him in the burning bush and sends him; he leads the people out with wonders and signs, receives living revelations at Sinai, and foretells a prophet like himself.

l: Joseph, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Joseph is sold into Egypt by the patriarchs out of jealousy, but God is with him and delivers him from his afflictions. He gains favor and wisdom before Pharaoh and is made governor over Egypt and Pharaoh's house. He is made known to his brothers on their second visit and summons Jacob and seventy-five relatives to Egypt.

l: Israelites (our fathers), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: The fathers sold Joseph, went to Egypt in famine, multiplied there, and were later mistreated and forced to abandon their babies. They rejected Moses, turned back in their hearts to Egypt, made a calf and worshiped it, and took up the tabernacle of Moloch. They had the tabernacle of the testimony, brought it in with Joshua, and persecuted the prophets, as Stephen says his hearers now do.

l: Egypt, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Egypt is where Joseph is made governor and where famine brings Jacob's family for grain. Jacob and the fathers die there, and the people multiply until a king who did not know Joseph oppresses them. Moses grows up there and later leads the people out through wonders and signs, though the fathers' hearts turn back to it.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Jesus is seen by Stephen standing at the right hand of God, whom Stephen calls the Son of Man. Stephen calls on him as Lord, asking him to receive his spirit. He is also referred to as the Righteous One whom the council has betrayed and murdered.

l: temple, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: Stephen says David asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob, but Solomon built the house. He declares that the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, citing the prophet's words that heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool.

l: Stephen's accusers (the council), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
s: The high priest and his hearers are called stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears, resisters of the Holy Spirit, and betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One who failed to keep the law. They are cut to the heart and gnash their teeth. They cry out, stop their ears, rush at Stephen, and throw him out of the city.

l: stoning of Stephen, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7
